At 7:42 this morning, a man named Dev ho: It took him half a second. By eight a.m., it will reach a nine-year-old he will never meet.
This is the butterfly effect... of a bad mood.
Meet Maya. Maya was having a perfectly nice morning. Then a car horn took about eleven years off her life.
She didn't know Dev. Didn't matter. His bad mood was hers now. Free of charge.
Degree one. Maya walks into her favorite café, carrying something she never ordered.
Leo the barista had been in a great mood. Had.
Psychologists call this emotional contagion. In one study, people who got a rude partner were later rated as rude by their next partner. Even when that next meeting came a week later.
Rudeness, it turns out, is a cold you catch from strangers.
Degree two. Enter Sam. Nine years old, paying for a hot chocolate entirely in coins.
Degree three. Three people. Eleven minutes. One horn.
And this is usually where the story ends. The mood keeps rolling, and nobody ever finds out where it started.
But Sam was about to do something nine-year-olds are weirdly good at.
Instead of passing the bad mood on, Sam passed on something else.
This is the ripple effect. Running backwards.
Leo cracked first.
Maya cracked second.
And at the crosswalk, Maya waves a car through. Guess whose.
Dev wasn't a monster. He was late for his daughter's first school play.
She was playing the butterfly. Obviously.

One study followed four thousand seven hundred people for twenty years. When someone you're directly connected to is happy, you're about fifteen percent more likely to be happy too. Their friends: almost ten percent. Their friends' friends: about six.
Three degrees. Strangers you'll never meet, feeling a little of what you feel.
You'll never meet most of the people your mood reaches. But every one of them will meet your mood.
So today, pass on a good one. Hold a door. Draw a terrible picture. Let someone cross.
Then tell us: who's in your three degrees? And if you spotted the butterfly... you know where to put it.
